# **Structural Variants for LLM Code Review in an Autonomous Merge Pipeline**

For standard 150-line, 6-file branches gated by one fresh-session Claude Opus 5.5 pass where fixed prompt and context overhead constitutes 73–96% of call cost, none of the four structural variants should replace the single-pass generalist review unconditionally. Based on available literature and break-even modeling, we recommend **do not adopt** for (a) multi-diff batching, **do not adopt** for (b) multi-call role-specialized panels on standard branches (folding conformance, defect, and security checklists into the single prompt instead), **adopt with changes** for (c) interleaved checkpoints (retaining 150-line branch-level checkpointing over milestone-end deferral while adding an upstream plan-review gate and rejecting sub-branch checkpoints), and **do not adopt** for (d) adversarial failing-test generation on standard branches.  
Empirical evidence isolating these exact architectures on frontier code review remains limited. No primary study directly measures per-diff recall and precision when batching multiple independent code diffs, compares a same-tier three-role panel (conformance, defects, security) against a structured generalist prompt, quantifies checkpoint versus end-of-branch agent review costs on long-horizon milestones, or benchmarks adversarial failing-test generation head-to-head against judgement review at the same model tier. Consequently, quantitative recommendations combine indirect code-review scaling measurements—most notably a 15-fold F1 collapse in single-diff LLM code review as diffs expand past 50–150 lines1—with adjacent batch-prompting benchmarks, multi-agent ablations, and Meta's production catching-test deployment (which exhibited an 80.5% post-filter false-positive rate)3.

## **1\. Batched Review of Independent Diffs**

**Direct code-review evidence: no evidence found.** Neither peer-reviewed studies, preprints, nor production engineering reports in the retrieved literature measure per-diff defect recall or precision when multiple independent diffs are evaluated in a single LLM call—or sequentially inside one shared session—compared against reviewing each diff in a separate fresh call. What is missing is a controlled experiment varying the number of independent diffs *k* and per-diff line count *L* inside one review prompt (or cumulative session) while measuring per-diff F1, recall, precision, and positional bias.  
Evidence from non-code-review batch prompting and single-diff scaling nevertheless establishes consistent degradation mechanisms as context items multiply. \[Peer-reviewed\] In *Batched Self-Consistency Improves LLM Relevance Assessment and Ranking* (Anton Korikov, Pan Du, Scott Sanner, and Navid Rekabsaz, 2025, EMNLP 2025 per filename emnlp25\_batchllm.pdf, https\://ssanner.github.io/papers/emnlp25\_batchllm.pdf), batching 10, 30, or 90 candidate passages made one-by-one pointwise ranking 15.3× slower on legal search, yet single-call batching (*m* \= 1\) did not beat separate evaluation (GPT-4o Legal Search NDCG@10 was 43.8% batched vs. 44.9% one-by-one); batching outperformed separate scoring by 5%–10% AUC-PR on Legal Search Shallow (and reached 51.3% vs. 46.8% NDCG@10 on GPT-4o) only when paired with *m* \= 15 shuffled self-consistency calls, while reporting no quantitative lost-in-the-middle breakdown5. \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] A secondary synthesis of batch prompting (https\://www\.emergentmind.com/topics/batch-prompting, citing Cheng et al. 2023 and Lin et al. 2023\) notes that prefix amortization reduces input tokens from n × (P \+ E\[\|q\|\]) to P \+ n × E\[\|q\|\], but observes U-shaped positional sensitivity and accuracy loss beyond batch sizes of 4–8 unless paired with permutation ensembling6. \[Preprint/peer-reviewed status unconfirmed in available text\] In https\://openreview.net/forum?id=Agyicd577r (title and authors truncated in extract; corresponding to BatchPrompt \+ BPE \+ SEAS, Lin et al. 2023 per secondary citations6), maintaining BoolQ accuracy at batch size 32 (90.6% to 90.9%, using 27.4% of baseline tokens) required Batch Permutation and Ensembling plus early stopping, consuming 15.7% of single-item LLM calls rather than a single batched pass8.  
Three further studies document positional and cross-item interference inside batched prompts. \[Peer-reviewed\] *Lost in Choice: Evaluating LLMs Under Extreme Multiple-Choice Scaling* (Association for Computational Linguistics, Findings of EMNLP 2026, Oct 24–29, 2026, pp. 6931–6963, https\://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-emnlp.328.pdf, Abstract and Section 3; author list not present in extract) evaluates 31,000 MMLU-XT instances and ToolBench trajectories—backed by a 200-pair audit (κ \= 0.82) showing 94.0% weakest-domain precision and \<4.5% global FNR—and finds accuracy collapses asymmetrically at late-middle and terminal positions rather than recovering in a U-shape9. \[Peer-reviewed\] Another ACL Findings of EMNLP 2026 paper (https\://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-emnlp.119.pdf, p. 2464, Figures 2–3; title and authors not present in extract) testing batch sizes 1–128 on GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini reports that conventional single-call batch prompting underperforms unpredictably relative to single-item prompting, and even cascaded batching (peaking at 86.81% MMLU and 86.20% MNLI on GPT-4.1-mini) slightly degrades by batch size 12810. \[Preprint\] In BatchSafeBench (*Efficient but Vulnerable: Benchmarking and Defending LLM Batch Prompting Attack*, 2025, https\://arxiv.org/html/2503.15551, Table 1 and Results; authors not listed in extract, title matched via6), evaluating 8,000 batched instances showed GPT-4 series models suffer \>90% average attack success rate from cross-item interference (88.8% for GPT-4o at batch size 20), and even benign-looking content appends cut accuracy by 0.5%–6% on GSM8k and 2%–13% on HotpotQA11. Sequential multi-diff review inside one persistent session faces related context-bloat failure modes noted qualitatively in agent engineering posts12.  
For code review specifically, the closest quantitative proxy is diff-size scaling inside one prompt. \[Preprint\] In *Bigger Isn't Always Better: A Comparative Evaluation of LLMs for Automated Code Review* (Shivam Pankaj Kumar, Swati Bararia, and Kislay Raj, April 9, 2026, https\://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.15689, Abstract, Section 3, and Section 4.5 / Figure 3), across 150 samples (100 synthetic mutations with median 5 and max 40 lines; 50 real GitHub PRs with median 117 and max 562 lines across 1–10 files), Claude Haiku 4.5's F1 falls from 0.657 on tiny diffs (\<10 lines, n \= 92\) and 0.800 on small diffs (10–50 lines, n \= 10\) to 0.070 on medium diffs (50–150 lines, n \= 34\) and 0.043 on large diffs (150–600 lines, n \= 14)—a 15-fold drop from small to large diffs reported in Figure 3, and a 92% collapse from synthetic diffs (F1 \= 0.847) to real PRs alone (best F1 \= 0.066)1.

**\[Inference\]** Under cited parameters, batching loses across standard 150-line branches and remains marginal even on small diffs. First, on 150-line diffs, batching just *k* \= 2 puts 300 changed lines in context; extrapolating from Kumar et al.'s single-diff drop from Medium (50–150 lines, F1 \= 0.070) to Large (150–600 lines, F1 \= 0.043) yields a **38.6% relative F1 loss**1, already exceeding the 36.5% lower-bound savings at *s* \= 0.73 before counting escape penalties (though independent diffs avoid cross-file coupling and may lose less than single PRs). Second, escape-cost asymmetry shrinks tolerable recall loss to near zero: \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] newmarketpitch.com (2026, https\://newmarketpitch.com/blogs/news/ai-code-assistant-agents-too-expensive) reports Claude Opus 5.5 list prices around \$4/M input and \$20/M output (and self-hosted PR-Agent reviews run $0.02–$0.25 per baeseokjae.github.io14), placing *F* around \~$0.05–$0.30, whereas senior debugging and rework of an escaped AI patch is estimated at $300–$450 (2–3 hrs at $150/hr)or~$500 (3.3 hrs)15. Even with baseline recall ![][image15]1 and 20% defect rate (![][image16]), ![][image17] and ![][image18] yields ![][image19], permitting at most **0.33%–0.58%** relative recall loss across *k* \= 2–8; even if automated local rework catches escaped bugs for only \$20 (![][image20]), tolerable recall loss is **5.0%–7.5%**, below the 0.5%–13% interference drops observed in BatchSafeBench11. The narrowest theoretical window where batching could help is *k* \= 2 tiny diffs of 10–25 lines each (staying within the 10–50 line sweet spot where Kumar et al. measured F1 \= 0.800)1.

## **2\. Role-Specialized Single-Pass Panels**

**Evidence by objective (same-tier dedicated vs. generalist):** Evaluating the three requested objectives reveals unequal coverage across the literature. For **plan/goal conformance**, **no evidence found** comparing a dedicated conformance-review prompt against a generalist diff prompt at the same model tier with F1, recall, or precision; \[Preprint\] https\://arxiv.org/html/2609.01087v1 (title and authors not present in extract; 2026 per ID) shows supervised fine-tuning of GPT-4o, CodeLlama-7B, and CodeQwen1.5 improves PR–issue alignment classification qualitatively, without reporting benchmark metrics against a generalist review16. For **defect detection**, **no direct same-tier generalist vs. single-objective defect prompt benchmark was found**; in \[Preprint\] CodeX-Verify (https\://arxiv.org/html/2511.16708v1, Nov 2025, Section 6.2; Shreshth Rajan per official repo https\://github.com/ShreshthRajan/codex-verify, full paper title absent from extract), four specialized agents (Correctness, Security, Performance, Style) operating without code execution at sub-200 ms latency averaged 32.8% accuracy individually (ranging 17.2%–75.9% across 99 labeled SWE-bench failure samples in 16 categories) against a 40% Codex baseline, without isolating Correctness F1 against a generalist prompt17. Indirectly, Table 6 of Kumar et al. (arXiv:2606.15689, n \= 1501) confirms a single generalist prompt struggles heavily on non-security defects, capturing 12.7%–24.5% of logic bugs (Haiku 4.5 24.5%, Sonnet 4.6 19.6%), 13.6%–33.3% of architecture bugs, 0.0%–6.7% of best-practice issues, and 0.0%–4.5% of performance bugs.  
For **security**, dedicated structured workflows measurably beat generic same-tier baselines. \[Preprint\] In VIC-RAGENT (https\://arxiv.org/html/2607.05772v1, July 2026 per ID, Table 3 and ablation; title and authors not listed in extract), prompting the same underlying LLM to check commits against 25 predefined vulnerability factors lifted F1 on DeepSeek-V3.2 to **57% vs. 33%** for CodeAgent, whereas Chain-of-Thought achieved 86% precision at only 6% recall (and Direct prompting lagged VIC-RAGENT across DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-4o-mini, and Qwen-Plus); dropping the Stage 3 final verification step raised false positives from 22 to 30 and cut true negatives from 113 to 10519. \[Preprint, cited via arXiv:2511.16708\] Yujia Chen's *AutoReview: An LLM-based Multi-Agent System for Security Issue-Oriented Code Review* (July 28, 2025, https\://www\.researchgate.net/publication/394078105\_AutoReview\_An\_LLM-based\_Multi-Agent\_System\_for\_Security\_Issue-Oriented\_Code\_Review) increased security F1 by **\+18.72%** on ReposVul20. \[Preprint/unverified listing\] A separate seven-agent CLI system, *A Multi-Agent System for Automated Pre-Push Code Review* (AutoReview CLI, https\://www\.researchgate.net/publication/397984834\_A\_Multi-Agent\_System\_for\_Automated\_Pre-Push\_Code\_Review, Section 5.1–5.2 and Tables 1–2; authors and date not shown in extract), evaluated 200 changesets across 5 projects and reported **78% recall** vs. **55%** for manual review in 58 seconds (\$0.34/review), with its Security Agent finding **91%** of ground-truth security vulnerabilities (+87% critical security detection, p \< 0.001), Security \+ Quality \+ Testing capturing 73% of critical findings, and Performance \+ Architecture finding 94% of performance-critical issues despite contributing 18% of findings—yet it did not benchmark a single generalist LLM prompt22. Meanwhile, generalist prompts in Kumar et al. (arXiv:2606.15689, Table 61) already attained **69.6%–71.1%** security recall across five models.  
Sources diverge sharply on when combining multiple reviewers beats a single reviewer, depending on error independence and verification gating. When specialized agents exhibit low pairwise error correlation (ρ \= 0.05–0.25 in CodeX-Verify Table 3), combining them yields diminishing yet substantial accuracy gains: 32.8% (1-agent avg) → 47.7% (+14.9 pp, 2 agents) → 61.2% (+13.5 pp, 3 agents) → 72.4% (+11.2 pp, 4 agents), with \[Secondary synthesis\] https\://www\.emergentmind.com/topics/codex-verify reporting the best 2-agent pair (Correctness \+ Performance) at 79.3% accuracy (83.3% TPR, 40.0% FPR) vs. 75.9% for the strongest single agent17. Crucially, naive union in CodeX-Verify yielded an **80% FPR** (75% TPR); calibrated severity weighting (0.45, 0.35, 0.15, 0.05 vs. uniform 0.25) improved F1 from 0.65 to 0.78, yet final FPR remained **50.0%** at 76.1% TPR (68.7% ± 9.1% accuracy)17. Similarly, \[Preprint\] *Adversarial Review: Structured Disagreement for Grounded Agentic Code Review* (Cornell and Stanford, https\://openreview.net/pdf?id=fOHvpLs6zp, Table 1 and Section 4.5; full author list and date truncated in extract) found that pairing a reviewer with an evidence-enforcing critic (3 agents) achieved **87%** pass rate on LiveCodeBench (75% on hard tasks) and **F1 \= 0.533** on diff review—whereas an ungrounded "Two-reviewers" panel (3 agents) *dropped* pass rate from 77% (Zero-shot / Single-reviewer) to **75%** (60% on hard tasks) due to sycophantic false agreement24. Likewise, Kumar et al. (arXiv:2606.15689, Section 4.7 / Table 91) reported that pairing two different models on the same generalist prompt lowered F1 from **0.365** (Haiku 4.5 alone: P \= 0.486, R \= 0.293) to **0.333** (Haiku ∪ Sonnet 4.6: P \= 0.627, R \= 0.226) and **0.304** (Haiku ∪ GLM-5 Turbo: P \= 0.694, R \= 0.195), with 55/150 samples (36.7%) flagged by all five models and 19/150 (12.7%) missed by all—though the simultaneous rise in precision and drop in recall under ∪ suggests an undocumented consensus/filtering step in Table 9 rather than raw set union. \[Peer-reviewed\] Finally, on deterministic probe-bounded crypto dependency transitions (CryptoUpdate-Mini-30), MDPI *Computers* 2026, 15(9), 638 (https\://www\.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/9/638, Section 4.1 / Table 5; title and authors not in extract) found that single-agent and Planner–Verifier matched the full multi-agent VeriCrypt-Agent on transition macro-F1 (though routing 24/30 vs. 9/30 runs to review), while an exhaustive deterministic probe gate outperformed all LLM variants (10/10 correct transitions)25.  
Commercial benchmarks and engineering posts reinforce the role of a verification pass to control false positives. \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] Bae Seokjae (https\://baeseokjae.github.io/posts/qodo-review-2026/, 2026\) cites independent benchmarks showing Qodo 2.0's February 2026 multi-agent architecture at **60.1% F1** (under its \~800-line truncation limit) vs. \~54% bug catch rate for GitHub Copilot14, while \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] MorphLLM (https\://www\.morphllm.com/comparisons/greptile-vs-copilot, March 14, 2026\) reports Greptile at **50.2% F1** (66.2% precision, 40.4% recall) vs. Copilot at **44.5% F1** (56.5% precision, 36.7% recall) on separate leaderboard evaluations26. \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] G-Research (https\://www\.gresearch.com/news/building-a-code-review-tool-the-llm-patterns-that-actually-work/) found single-pass review produced \~8 findings with 2–3 false positives and solved this by splitting recall generation and precision filtering into two sequential passes ("two simple passes outperform one complex prompt"), achieving \>85% precision thresholds in integration tests27.  
**Duplicate-finding rate, cost multiplier, and conformance model downgrade:** **No evidence found** measuring exact duplicate-finding rates across conformance, defect, and security passes (the closest proxy is Kumar et al.'s 36.7% five-model overlap1, and skmdroid/quorum28 plus Ashishkosana/review-lens29 note that deduplicating synthesizers or adversarial verify steps are required). **No evidence found** directly testing whether a conformance-only pass can be downgraded to a cheaper model tier. Indirect model-tier results conflict: without tool grounding, Haiku 4.5 ($0.003/review)beatSonnet4.6($0.010/review) on recall (0.293 vs. 0.248, \+18.1%) and F1 (0.365 vs. 0.343) in Kumar et al. (arXiv:2606.15689, Table 51), while Sonnet 4.6 retained higher precision (0.558 vs. 0.486) and severity-weighted F1 (0.543 vs. 0.485); conversely, when grounded in Ruff, ESLint, Semgrep, and Bandit outputs (\[Preprint\] https\://www\.researchgate.net/publication/416504011\_A\_Multi-Agent\_Framework\_for\_Evidence-Grounded\_Automated\_Code\_Review, Section 330), GPT-4o-mini nearly matched GPT-4-Turbo-preview (97.83% precision / 52.94% recall vs. 100% / 55.56% at 33.0 s avg), whereas Claude-3-Haiku-20241022 dropped to 96.15% actionability / 47.22% recall. **\[Inference\]** Under fixed-cost-dominated billing, running three separate single-pass reviews at Opus 5.5 tier costs **3.0×** baseline (plus synthesis overhead); downgrading the conformance pass to Sonnet 5.5 ($2/$10 vs. Opus 5.5 $4/$20\) or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.30/$1.20) per newmarketpitch.com list prices15 cuts total review cost to **2.50×** or **\~2.07×**, respectively.

## **3\. Interleaved Per-Task Checkpoints vs. End-of-Branch Review**

**Controlled empirical comparison: no evidence found.** No study in the retrieved literature directly compares per-checkpoint LLM code review against end-of-branch LLM review on identical multi-task coding-agent workloads with measurements of drift rate, accumulated-defect detection, or cost per accepted-and-correct milestone.  
Indirect quantitative measurements point consistently toward smaller, checkpointed diffs and independent reviewer sessions. First, Kumar et al.'s diff-size curve (arXiv:2606.15689, Section 4.5 / Figure 31) shows F1 collapsing from **0.800** (10–50 lines) and **0.657** (\<10 lines) to **0.070** (50–150 lines) and **0.043** (150–600 lines) due to formatting noise and multi-file interactions1. **\[Inference\]** Deferring two 150-line branches into one 300-line milestone-end review pushes the diff squarely into the 150–600 line failure regime (an inferred 38.6% drop relative to 50–150 lines) while allowing step-2 edits to compound defects introduced in step 1\. Second, \[Preprint\] an empirical analysis of 278,790 inline review conversations across 300 GitHub projects (https\://arxiv.org/html/2603.15911v2, March 2026 per ID, RQ2 and Fig. 5; title and authors not in extract) found human reviews of AI-generated code require **11.8% more back-and-forth exchange rounds** than human code, while \>95% of AI reviewer comments target Code Improvement and Defect Detection (Cursor 99% defect detection vs. Claude Code 20% vs. 40% agent average)31. \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] CodeRabbit's analysis of 470 PRs (https\://www\.coderabbit.ai/guides/coding-agent-workflow) similarly reports AI co-authored PRs averaged **10.83 issues vs. 6.45** for human-only PRs32. Third, \[Preprint summary via Hugging Face Papers\] (https\://huggingface.co/papers?q=review%20agent, full citation truncated in search listing) reports LLMs fail to disclose synthetic mistakes prefilled into trajectories in **36.4%** of chat rollouts and **67.1%** of agentic rollouts, reinforcing practitioner evidence (https\://medium.com/@pvginkel/my-ai-workflow-part-7-running-slices-with-pre-flight-and-verification-4d5812d42c90) that checkpoint reviews must run in a fresh reviewer session rather than inside the generator's context33.  
On **fix-cost asymmetry**, **no peer-reviewed empirical measurements were found** comparing defects caught at an agent checkpoint versus at milestone completion. Only unrefereed practitioner and industry estimates exist: \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] a post on dev.to (https\://dev.to/gde/giving-ai-pain-the-architecture-of-synthetic-scars-the-rapid-regret-miner-1740) asserts across 238 production tickets (without presenting an audited cost ledger in the extract) that Boehm's Cost-of-Defect curve translates to **\$1 : \$500 : \$25,000** across stages35, while newmarketpitch.com estimates that a few dollars of coding-agent tokens can trigger $300–$**450** (2–3 hours) to **\~\$500** (3.3 hours) of senior engineering rework at \$150/hour15.  
**\[Inference\] Cost Multiplier across Checkpoint Granularities:** Retaining the pipeline's current **branch-level checkpoints** (two separate 150-line reviews vs. one 300-line milestone-end review) incurs a review-call multiplier of ![][image21] **1.57×** (at *s* \= 0.73) to **1.92×** (at *s* \= 0.96), or **1.95× to 2.78×** for three 150-line branches vs. one 450-line diff. By contrast, adding *intra-branch* sub-checkpoints—such as pausing for three 50-line Opus 5.5 reviews inside one 150-line branch—multiplies review cost by ![][image22] **2.46× to 2.92×** while stalling the single local Qwen 3.8 GPU inference slot between edits.  
For **plan-review-then-diff-review pipelines**, architectural reports define clear stage responsibilities, though **no evidence found** reporting empirical defect-detection shares (recall/F1) broken out by stage:

| Pipeline Stage | Defect Classes Targeted | Sources & Epistemic Status |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Pre-Code Plan Review** | Architecturally off-target designs, overly narrow fixes, unspecified component contracts (types, error codes, versioning), missing negative/failure paths (timeouts, partial failures, races), circular dependencies, insecure defaults, and spec ambiguity | \[Preprint\] Seven-stage loop (https\://arxiv.org/html/2605.22794v1, May 2026 per ID)36; \[Vendor/practitioner blogs\] plan-swarm-review37, Elephant-Goldfish38, curohq.com39, aalpha.net40 |
| **Checkpoint Diff Review** | Local logic/happy-path bugs, plan-to-code divergence before later tasks depend on flawed abstractions, and out-of-scope edits | \[Preprint\] arXiv:2605.22794v1 (diff reviewed against approved plan, hard-reset on reject)36; \[Vendor/practitioner blogs\] review-checkpoint41, Hermes IDE turn review42, junie.jetbrains.com43 |
| **Cumulative / End-of-Milestone Check** | Cross-branch spec drift against immutable test contracts and multi-file or cross-package integration bugs invisible to single diffs | \[Vendor/practitioner blogs\] review-checkpoint cumulative \+ final verification41, Elephant-Goldfish Drift Check38, stack72.dev44 |

## **4\. Adversarial and Test-Generation Reviewers**

**Head-to-head yield vs. judgement review and cost per true defect: no evidence found.** No study benchmarks adversarial failing-test generation against single-pass judgement review at the same model tier on the same PR corpus, nor reports dollar or token cost per true defect found. However, primary peer-reviewed and preprint measurements quantify diff-level feasibility, catching-test yield, and oracle failure modes.  
\[Peer-reviewed\] Meta's *Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta* (Matthew Becker et al., 15 authors, arXiv Jan 30, 2026 / *Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE Companion '26)*, June 2026, pp. 282–293, https\://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22832 and https\://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.22832, Abstract and Sections 1–3) reports the largest industrial evaluation found, operating directly on **diffs** across backend systems of hundreds of millions of lines of code3. Rather than scanning entire repositories, Meta deployed two diff-aware workflows—generating tests on the parent revision from inferred diff intent, and using Meta's ACH generator to treat the diff itself as a mutant to kill—which required parent and child build/test execution4. Across **22,126 generated tests**, diff-aware workflows produced **\~4×** as many weak catches (tests passing on parent, failing on diff) as traditional coverage-hardening workflows and **\~20×** as many as a coincidental-failure baseline3. Because weak catches mostly reflect intended behavior changes, Meta manually studied **600 diffs with weak catches**, finding an LLM-as-judge ensemble (supplemented by rule-based RubFake in production) cut human review load by **\~70%** (\~4× capacity scaling)3. Even *after* that 70% filter, out of **41 engineer reach-outs**, only **8 were immediately confirmed as strong catches**—an **engineer-experienced true positive rate of 19.5%** (meaning **80.5% false positives** among filtered alerts), with **4 (9.8% of reach-outs)** averting serious production failures3. Dismissing false positives took engineers only a few minutes, though the authors explicitly emphasize that catching test generation is "inherently computationally expensive" because many tests must be generated per diff3. \[Vendor or practitioner blog\] Meta's October 29, 2026 engineering post (https\://engineering.fb.com/2026/10/29/security/catching-bugs-before-they-land-jittestings-human-on-the-loop-approach-at-full-scale/) details the production rollout46; secondary summaries of that post (https\://checkops.com/blog/meta-jittests-just-in-time-tests and https\://en.mundoia.com.ar/meta-ia-pruebas-errores-privacidad-jittests/) report **74 serious privacy bugs** caught at the diff stage in the first half of 202647. **\[Inference\]** Dividing Meta's 8 confirmed catches by the implied \~136.7 pre-filter candidates (41 / 0.30 surviving a \~70% judge reduction) suggests a raw pre-filter strong-catch yield near **\~5.9%**.  
Two major technical obstacles explain low standalone yields in LLM-generated catching tests. First, \[Preprint\] an empirical study across **145 PRs from SciPy, Qiskit, and pandas** (https\://arxiv.org/html/2610.11835v1, Oct 2026 per ID, Abstract and Answer to RQ1; title and authors not in extract) found only **2.4%–4.8%** of LLM-generated tests were fault-revealing, whereas **8.4%–16.9%** (8%–17% in Abstract)—**3.5–6.5× higher**—were **fault-enforcing**, encoding buggy diff behavior as expected truth (with 99.8% of comparable pairs asserting behavior introduced in the PR); 83%–91% persisted longitudinally and 83%–92% remained enforced when faults accumulated while existing suites caught only 14%–30%49. Only 5.2% (249 of 4,763) of invalid tests failed at import or collection; the vast majority executed and failed on both versions49. Second, \[Preprint\] a failure taxonomy comparing **263 AssertFlip** and **464 OpenHands** bug-reproduction tests (https\://arxiv.org/html/2611.13395v1, Nov 2026 per ID, RQ2, RQ3, and Table II; title and authors not in extract) recorded high mechanical and environment failure rates on GPT-4o-mini (OpenHands: **64.8% Mechanical Failure**, including **41.3% Environment Error**, plus **25.0% Misimplementations**; AssertFlip: **14.1% Mechanical Failure**, 0.0% Environment Error, **25.4% Misimplementations**), dropping on GPT-5-mini to **21.8% Mechanical Failure** and **15.1% Misimplementations** on OpenHands; issue augmentation resolved 7 of 11 previously failing cases50. Consistently, \[Preprint/thesis\] a University of Waterloo study (https\://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstreams/481ed117-08da-4c16-815b-23ea121afcb6/download, Section 2.2 and Results; author and date not in extract) measured open-source test accuracy on correct code alone at 22.93% (Llama-3.3-70B), 18.01% (Codestral-22B), and 11.94% (Llama-3.1-8B), confirming that pairing explicit requirements with code increases bug detection51. \[Secondary summary\] On PR review quality, PyPI's jittest summary (https\://pypi.org/project/jittest/) cites BSG-VA (arXiv:2607.28871, Xu & Wu, 2026), where differential test execution shifted evidence-inadequate PR closure by \+7.8 pp, below its 10 pp pre-registered threshold (\~1/3 attributable to reminder prompts)52.  
Compared qualitatively to judgement-style review—which reaches 48.6%–55.8% precision on mixed synthetic/real diffs (arXiv:2606.15689, albeit 0.066 real-PR F1)1, 56.5%–66.2% precision in commercial tools (morphllm.com)26, and 96.15%–100% precision with static-tool grounding (researchgate.net/publication/416504011)30—adversarial test generation has far lower raw precision (19.5% even post-LLM-judge) and misses non-executable architectural or style issues, yet delivers high-severity, concrete reproduction evidence when a true fault is hit3.

## **6\. Concrete Recommendations for the Standard-Branch Gate**

All quantitative projections below carry an explicit **\[Inference — Extrapolated\]** flag, because no cited primary source evaluates Claude Opus 5.5, Qwen 3.8 27B, or this exact 150-line / 6-file deterministic gate.

### **Variant (a) Batched Review: Do Not Adopt**

Do not batch multiple 150-line standard branches into one Opus 5.5 call or shared review session. \[Inference — Extrapolated\] Amortizing fixed cost *F* (*s* \= 0.73–0.96) across *k* \= 2–4 diffs cuts per-branch review API spend by **36.5%–72.0%**, but expands the reviewed diff to 300–600 lines. Extrapolating from arXiv:2606.15689's Haiku 4.5 single-diff buckets (0.070 F1 at 50–150 lines to 0.043 at 150–600 lines) implies up to a **38.6% F1 penalty**1, alongside cross-item accuracy interference (0.5%–13% in BatchSafeBench11) and terminal/middle positional decay6. Because downstream rework or bad-merge recovery (![][image11], estimated at $300–$500 in newmarketpitch.com for senior review15) exceeds sub-dollar per-call savings by one to three orders of magnitude, even a **0.3%–7.5% relative recall loss** raises cost per accepted-and-correct merge while serializing branches ahead of Qwen 3.8's single GPU slot.

### **Variant (b) Role-Specialized Single-Pass Panels: Do Not Adopt**

Do not split standard-branch Opus 5.5 reviews into three separate calls for plan conformance, defects, and security. \[Inference — Extrapolated\] Under fixed-cost dominance, three same-tier calls triple review spend to **3.0×** baseline (or **2.50×** with conformance on Sonnet 5.5 and **\~2.07×** on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, extrapolated from newmarketpitch.com list prices15), before counting deduplication overhead. Because no evidence demonstrates that three separate calls outperform one structured generalist frontier prompt containing dedicated conformance, defect, and security sections—and multi-agent aggregation without filtering caused 50%–80% false-positive rates in CodeX-Verify (arXiv:2511.16708v117)—expected cost per accepted-and-correct merge worsens by **\+107% to \+200%** for unvalidated recall gains. Keep a **1.0×** structured multi-lens single prompt on standard branches, and reserve a second precision-filtering pass (per G-Research27 and VIC-RAGENT19) or specialist split strictly for **elevated** branches.

### **Variant (c) Interleaved Checkpoints vs. End-of-Branch Review: Adopt with Changes**

Keep **branch-level checkpointing** (\~150 lines) rather than deferring review to end-of-milestone, **add** one fresh Opus 5.5 **Plan-Review** call upstream of Qwen 3.8 execution for multi-branch milestones, and **do not adopt** intra-branch sub-checkpoints inside a 150-line branch. \[Inference — Extrapolated\] Retaining per-branch review over a 300-line milestone-end diff costs **1.57×–1.92×** in review calls (extrapolated from *s* ∈ \[0.73, 0.96\]), yet avoids the \>150-line F1 \= 0.043 cliff (arXiv:2606.156891) and prevents downstream branches from amplifying flawed interfaces. Upstream plan review targets architectural, contract, and failure-mode defects (arXiv:2605.22794v136) before consuming local GPU inference, lowering total rework cost per milestone. Conversely, intra-branch 50-line checkpoints inflate fixed-cost review spend to **2.46×–2.92×** and stall the single GPU slot; when extra recall is needed, prefer decomposing work into smaller \~50-line independent branches (toward the 10–50 line F1 \= 0.800 sweet spot1).

### **Variant (d) Adversarial / Test-Generation Reviewers: Do Not Adopt**

Do not deploy failing-test generation on standard branches. \[Inference — Extrapolated\] Meta's Catching JiTTests (arXiv:2601.228323) shows diff-aware catching tests prevent high-severity outages (4 of 8 confirmed catches; 74 privacy bugs reported in H1 2026 via secondary summaries47), but only after multi-sample test generation, parent/child test execution, and a 70% LLM-judge filter—which still left an **80.5% false-positive rate** (19.5% TPR), while arXiv:2610.11835v1 found **8.4%–16.9%** of generated tests became fault-enforcing49. On standard 150-line branches, false test failures would trigger costly local Qwen 3.8 rework loops and sharply increase cost per accepted-and-correct merge. If adopted later, confine adversarial catching-test generation to **elevated** branches, ground prompts in explicit acceptance criteria (uwspace.uwaterloo.ca51), filter outputs with an LLM-judge, and discard failing tests after verification rather than committing them47.

## **7\. Least-Certain Claims**

> 1. **Extrapolating arXiv:2606.15689 single-PR diff scaling to batched independent diffs and Claude Opus 5.5:** The 38.6% F1 drop from 50–150 lines (0.070) to 150–600 lines (0.043) and 0.800 peak at 10–50 lines (n \= 10\) were measured on Claude Haiku 4.5 over single multi-file PRs, not on Opus 5.5 reviewing concatenated independent diffs1.  
> 2. **Table 9 ensemble behavior in arXiv:2606.15689:** Table 9 labels model pairings with union (∪) while precision rises (0.486 to 0.627–0.694) and recall drops (0.293 to 0.195–0.226), contradicting raw set union and indicating an unstated intersection or filtering step1.  
> 3. **Unbenchmarked standard-branch panel, conformance-downgrade, and checkpoint cost projections:** Expected multipliers for 3-role panels (2.07×–3.0×), milestone-end savings vs. branch checkpoints (1.57×–1.92×), and conformance tier downgrades derive from fixed-cost algebra and newmarketpitch.com list prices15 rather than empirical trials, with no direct benchmark of duplicate-finding rates or same-tier structured generalist prompts.  
> 4. **Practitioner defect-escape rework ratios:** The \$1 : \$500 : \$25,000 Boehm translation (dev.to/gde35) and $300–$500 senior debugging rework figures (newmarketpitch.com15) come from unrefereed practitioner/industry estimates without independently audited financial ledgers.  
> 5. **Secondary and unattributed commercial/benchmark figures:** Commercial tool comparisons (Greptile 50.2% vs. Copilot 44.5% F1 on morphllm.com26; Qodo 2.0 60.1% F1 vs. Copilot \~54% bug catch on baeseokjae.github.io14), Meta's H1 2026 figure of 74 privacy bugs (checkops.com47, mundoia48), and our inferred \~5.9% pre-filter strong-catch yield for Meta JiTTests3 rely on vendor posts, secondary summaries, or back-calculation across non-identical test beds.
